newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU warns WTO facing "immeasurable damage" from U.S.
newsitem.headline: EU warns WTO facing "immeasurable damage" from U.S.

text.p: European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan warned on Wednesday that a U.S. threat to ignore a World Trade Organisation ruling on the grounds of national security could immeasurably damage the procedure.
"Of course if national security is really involved, action may be permissible which would otherwise be contrary to normal trade rules," he said in a statement.

"But no country should be allowed to be judge and jury in its own cause. The dispute settlement mechanism ... must be entitled to consider whether the invocation of national security is reasonable in any given case. If not, the entire WTO dispute settlement process will be immeasurably damaged."

Brittan statement was seen by analysts as cranking up the pressure on the United States not to invoke national security in defence of a complaint at the WTO by the EU over Washington's Helms-Burton Act.

The act, an amalgamation of decades of Washington's anti-Cuba policy, among other things allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign individuals or companies benefiting from investments in property confiscated by Havana since the communist revolution of 1959.

Although U.S. president Bill Clinton has twice suspended this part for six months -- the last time in January -- the EU has nevertheless drafted counter laws and has proceeded with a complaint at the WTO.
On Wednesday Brittan said he had asked WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero to postpone naming a panel to rule on the issue for a week to allow more time for talks with Washington.

Washington has refused to discuss the composition of the three-person panel and last week Brittan called for Ruggiero to intervene personally. Brittan's request -- almost certain to be heeded -- means the panel will be named on February 20 unless the two sides settle their differnces.
"The European Union is as eager as the United States to resolve the dispute over the Helms-Burton Act," Brittan said. "The EU does not want litigation for its own sake.
Brittan said he had been involved in intensive contacts with the U.S. administration on the issue, but admitted only limited progress.
"We have no desire to take our case to the point of decision by a panel for its own sake," Brittan said. "It is not acceptable to say this issue is too sensitive for the WTO to handle."
In his statement, Brittan said to suggest that protection of national security requires interference in the legitimate trade of European companies with Cuba was "not credible".

"For the WTO to be effective, he said "it must not be possible for one country to evade its operation simply by proclaiming that national security is involved, however far-fetched such a claim may be".
